The '''1680 Ayuman Cup''', recognised retrospectively as the 6th edition of the '''[[FLLA World Cup]]''', was an international [[Arraby]] tournament contested by the senior men's national teams of the leading Ayuman football associations. It was held in [[Lycroa]], across [[Ayuma]], from 8 June to 7 July 1680, and was won by the hosts, [[Lycroa]], who drew the [[#Final|final]] with [[Eldjo]] 0–0 at the Jungui Grand Stadium and took the title on the toss of a coin to claim their third championship.<ref name="heritage-overview">{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/heritage/world-cup/1680/overview|title=The 1680 Ayuman Cup: tournament overview|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=9 June 1763}}</ref>

The 1680 final remains the only championship match in the history of the competition to have been decided by a coin toss. The [[wikipedia:Penalty shoot-out (association football)|penalty shoot-out]] had not yet been introduced, and under the regulations of the period a final still level after a single period of [[wikipedia:Extra time|extra time]] was to be settled by lot rather than replayed; with the scores goalless after 120 minutes, the organising officials tossed a coin at the centre of the pitch, and Lycroa won. The result has been the subject of recurring debate in the [[FLLA]]'s heritage records, which note that [[Eldjo]] remain the only side to reach a final without conceding a goal and yet finish as runners-up.<ref name="heritage-final">{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/heritage/world-cup/1680/final|title=The 1680 Ayuman Cup final: Lycroa 0–0 Eldjo, decided by coin toss|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=9 June 1763}}</ref>

It was staged under the older title of the Ayuman Cup, the name the competition bore before the [[FLLA]] was constituted and the contest was relaunched and renamed the [[FLLA World Cup]] at the [[1700 FLLA World Cup|1700 edition]]; the seven continental confederations did not yet exist, and the field was drawn overwhelmingly from [[Ayuma]], the [[Mahea]]n association of [[Taval]] again being among the entrants.<ref name="heritage-rename">{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/heritage/history/early-competition-names|title=From the Ayuman Cup to the FLLA World Cup: the early names of the competition|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=12 February 1764}}</ref>

The 1680 edition was contested for the original rotating '''[[FLLA World Cup#The Andah Cup|Andah Cup]]''', which had been awarded since its introduction at the [[1668 FLLA World Cup|1668 edition]] and which was presented to the victorious Lycroan side at the close of the final. No bespoke permanent trophy was commissioned in 1680; the permanent-trophy tradition that came to characterise the competition began only with the Solana at the [[1700 FLLA World Cup|1700 edition]], after the original cup was destroyed in [[Alzurian Union|Alzuria]] at the outbreak of the [[Red War]] in 1688.<ref name="heritage-trophy">{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/heritage/trophies/the-andah-cup|title=The original Andah Cup and its loss in 1688|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=2 July 1764}}</ref>

==Host selection==

The 1680 tournament was awarded to [[Lycroa]] by a congress of the Ayuman national associations, the informal body that organised the competition before the foundation of the [[FLLA]]. The award recognised the standing of the Lycroan game, twice champions in the preceding editions, and the hosting was presented at the time as an opportunity for the Lycroan associations to stage the leading sides of [[Ayuma]] in a single tournament. The Lycroan organisers undertook to hold the finals across five cities, with the principal matches played in [[Jungui]].<ref name="heritage-host">{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/heritage/world-cup/1680/host|title=1680 Ayuman Cup: the award of hosting rights to Lycroa|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=9 June 1763}}</ref>

==Format==

Thirteen teams entered the 1680 finals, an uneven number that produced a group stage of two groups of four and one group of five. Each group operated on a single round-robin basis, with each team playing the others in its group once; two points were awarded for a win and one for a draw, in line with the scoring system then in use. The top two teams in each group advanced to the [[#Knockout stage|knockout stage]], and the two best third-placed teams across the three groups completed the field of eight. Where teams finished level on points, places were determined first by goal difference and then by goals scored.

Because the five-team Group C played one more round of matches than the four-team groups, the congress ruled that, for the purpose of ranking the third-placed sides against one another, the results of the Group C third-placed team against the bottom side in its group would be set aside, so that each contending team was compared over three matches.

The knockout stage consisted of single-elimination ties played over 90 minutes. A tie level at the end of normal time was extended by a single 30-minute period of [[wikipedia:Extra time|extra time]]; under the regulations of the period, any tie still level after extra time was settled by lot rather than by a [[wikipedia:Penalty shoot-out (association football)|penalty shoot-out]], a procedure not yet in use. The provision was invoked only once, in the [[#Final|final]] itself, which was decided by the toss of a coin. The two losing semi-finalists contested a [[#Third place playoff|third-place playoff]] on the day before the final.

==Venues==

Five stadiums in five host cities, all in [[Lycroa]], were used in the final tournament. The principal venue was the Jungui Grand Stadium in [[Jungui]], which staged the opening match and the final and was the only ground with a capacity of 25,000. The two semi-finals were divided between the Liambra Arena in [[Liambra]] and the Sompai Stadium in [[Sompai]], with the [[#Third place playoff|third-place playoff]] held at Tianco Park in [[Tianco]]. The remaining group-stage fixtures were shared between these grounds and the smallest venue, at [[Zaringao]].<ref name="heritage-venues">{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/heritage/world-cup/1680/venues|title=Host stadiums of the 1680 Ayuman Cup|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=18 June 1763}}</ref>

==Squads==

Each participating association registered a squad of eighteen players, two of whom were required to be goalkeepers; the smaller squads of the period reflected the limited substitution rules then in force, under which a single replacement was permitted only for an injured goalkeeper. A total of 234 players were registered for the tournament.<ref name="heritage-squads">{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/heritage/world-cup/1680/squads|title=1680 Ayuman Cup: registered squads|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=18 June 1763}}</ref>

==Match officials==

The organising congress appointed a panel of referees and linesmen drawn from the associations not represented in the latter stages of the competition. The opening match was refereed by Joren Aldal of [[Verusa]], and the final by Halsten Vey of [[Yaxuto]], the senior official of the tournament. The small officiating pool of the period meant that several referees took charge of fixtures involving teams from neighbouring associations, though never from their own.<ref name="heritage-officials">{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/heritage/world-cup/1680/officials|title=Match officials of the 1680 Ayuman Cup|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=18 June 1763}}</ref>

==Group stage==

The groups were each contested as a single round-robin. The top two teams in each group advanced to the knockout stage, joined by the two best third-placed sides; points were awarded on the two-points-for-a-win system in use at the time, with goal difference and then goals scored used to separate teams level on points.

All dates are given in the local time of the host cities.

==Knockout stage==

The knockout stage involved the eight teams that advanced from the group stage. Ties level after 90 minutes were extended by a single period of [[wikipedia:Extra time|extra time]]; one of the four quarter-finals was decided in the additional period, and the [[#Final|final]] was settled by the toss of a coin after extra time failed to produce a goal. The bracket was arranged so that the two qualifiers from Group C, [[Lycroa]] and [[Eldjo]], were placed in opposite halves and could meet only in the final.

===Final===

The final was held at the Jungui Grand Stadium on 7 July 1680 before an estimated crowd of 25,000. The match was a tense and defensive affair: [[Lycroa]] and [[Eldjo]] could not be separated across 90 minutes, and a single period of extra time likewise produced no goal, leaving the tie level at 0–0. With the [[wikipedia:Penalty shoot-out (association football)|penalty shoot-out]] not yet in use, the regulations of the period required the championship to be decided by lot. The organising officials tossed a coin at the centre of the pitch, and Lycroa won, taking their third title and becoming the only side in the history of the competition to be crowned champions on a coin toss. The original [[FLLA World Cup#The Andah Cup|Andah Cup]] was presented to the Lycroan captain at the close of the match.<ref name="heritage-final" />

==Statistics==

===Goalscorers===

A total of 63 goals were scored in 30 matches, an average of 2.10 per match. The leading scorer was the Lycroan forward Davin Calmar, who scored six goals across the tournament, though he did not find the net in the goalless final. No formal individual awards were presented at the 1680 edition: the leading-player, top-scorer and best-goalkeeper prizes (the [[FLLA World Cup#Awards|Vairan Ball, Marskval and Bastion]]) were not instituted until the [[1744 FLLA World Cup|1744 edition]], and the figures below are recognised retrospectively in the [[FLLA]]'s heritage records.<ref name="heritage-stats">{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/heritage/world-cup/1680/statistics|title=1680 Ayuman Cup statistical record|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=18 June 1763}}</ref>

==Trophy and significance==

The 1680 edition holds a distinctive place in the history of the [[FLLA World Cup]] as the only championship to have been settled by the toss of a coin. The goalless final and its decision by lot have remained a recurring point of reference in accounts of the early competition, and the introduction of the [[wikipedia:Penalty shoot-out (association football)|penalty shoot-out]] in later editions is often traced to the controversy that the 1680 result provoked.<ref name="heritage-final" />

The cup that Lycroa lifted was the original rotating [[FLLA World Cup#The Andah Cup|Andah Cup]], which had been contested since its introduction at the [[1668 FLLA World Cup|1668 edition]]. It was awarded again at the [[1684 FLLA World Cup|1684 edition]] in [[Alzurian Union|Alzuria]], the last occasion on which the original trophy was presented; the cup was destroyed in Alzuria at the outbreak of the [[Red War]] in 1688. When the competition was relaunched and renamed the [[FLLA World Cup]] at the [[1700 FLLA World Cup|1700 edition]], no rotating cup was available, and the host association instead commissioned a bespoke permanent trophy, beginning the permanent-trophy tradition that has characterised the competition ever since.<ref name="heritage-trophy" />
